name: Quantitative Data
definition: Data expressed as numbers that measure or count something, so arithmetic on the values is meaningful.
example: Trip length in minutes and the fare in dollars for a bike-share trip.

name: Qualitative Data
definition: Data that describes qualities, categories or opinions, usually as words, labels, images or sounds.
example: A rider's comment that a dock was jammed, or the name of a docking station.

name: Levels of Measurement
definition: The four scales that describe how much information a variable carries: nominal (names), ordinal (order), interval (equal gaps) and ratio (equal gaps and a true zero).
example: Station name is nominal, a 1 to 5 star rating is ordinal, temperature in degrees Celsius is interval and trip minutes are ratio.

name: Stratified Sampling
definition: A sampling method that divides the population into groups (strata) and samples each group in proportion to its size.
example: Surveying 20 of 200 members and 40 of 400 casual riders, so both groups are represented.

name: Passive Data Collection
definition: Capturing data as a by-product of what people do, without them deliberately providing it.
example: Dock sensors and GPS logs recording every bike trip.

name: Primary Data
definition: Data collected first-hand by an enterprise for its own purpose.
example: A bike-share's own trip log or its rider survey.

name: Secondary Data
definition: Data that was collected by someone else, usually for a different purpose, and is reused.
example: Daily rainfall figures from the Bureau of Meteorology used to study bike demand.

name: Informatics
definition: The science of processing data for storage and retrieval, used to turn raw data into information that people can understand and act on.
example: Organising a bike-share's trip records into tables, summarising them and presenting a dashboard to the operations manager.

name: Unstructured Data
definition: Data with no predefined model or field layout, such as free text, images, audio and video.
example: Rider comments, photos of damaged bikes and recorded customer calls.

name: Alternative Data
definition: Data from non-traditional sources, such as likes, emoticons and memes, used as quick feedback about a product or message.
example: A surge of angry-face reactions on a post about a new e-bike.

name: Data Bias
definition: A systematic tilt in how data is collected, analysed or used, so that results consistently lean in one direction.
example: Surveying only app users, so riders without smartphones are missing from the results.

name: Blockchain
definition: A growing list of records, called blocks, linked using cryptography so that any change to an earlier block is detectable.
example: Each block stores the hash of the previous block, so editing one block breaks every later link.

name: Hash Function
definition: A function that turns any input into a fixed-length output (a hash) that changes completely if the input changes and cannot practically be reversed.
example: SHA-256 turns a block of transactions into a 64-character fingerprint.

name: Distributed Ledger
definition: A record of transactions held as identical copies on many computers (nodes), with no single master copy.
example: Every node in a public blockchain stores the full chain of blocks.

name: Consensus Mechanism
definition: The rule a distributed network uses to agree on which new block or record is valid.
example: Proof of work and proof of stake are two consensus mechanisms.

name: Big Data
definition: Extremely large datasets that may be analysed computationally to reveal patterns, trends and associations, often described by their volume, variety and velocity.
example: A GPS point logged every few seconds for every bike in a scheme.

name: Data Mining
definition: Discovering patterns, relationships and unusual values in large datasets using statistics and machine learning.
example: Finding groups of riders with similar travel habits so that passes can be designed for each.

name: Metadata
definition: A set of data that describes and gives information about other data.
example: A photo's file details, such as when and where it was taken and its copyright.

name: Data Swamp
definition: A data lake that has become unusable because nothing records what the data is, where it came from, its quality or who owns it.
example: A store of thousands of unlabelled, duplicate files that analysts cannot trust.

name: Data Literacy
definition: The ability to read, understand, question and communicate with data.
example: Checking who collected a chart's data, how big the sample was and whether the axis starts at zero.

name: CARE Principles
definition: Principles for Indigenous data governance from the Global Indigenous Data Alliance: Collective benefit, Authority to control, Responsibility and Ethics.
example: A research team agrees with an Aboriginal community-controlled organisation how its data will be stored and shared.

name: Slicer
definition: A set of buttons in a spreadsheet dashboard that filters connected pivot tables and charts without changing the source data.
example: Clicking Riverside Park in a station slicer to show only that station's figures.

name: Flat-File Database
definition: A database that stores all its data in a single table of records and fields.
example: A single table of trips that repeats each rider's name on every row.

name: Relational Database
definition: A database that stores data in several linked tables, using primary and foreign keys, so each fact is stored once.
example: Separate Riders, Bikes, Stations and Trips tables linked by RiderID, BikeID and StationID.
